tour.title: When Prayer Won’t Come: A Tour Through Grief
tour.intro: Your mother died only three weeks ago, and this tour will not ask you to tidy that grief away. It begins with someone speaking directly to the silence and doubt that can make prayer feel impossible, then gives you language for lament, stays with Jesus’ own tears, and only afterward considers comfort and hope. You do not need to force yourself to feel better or turn these clips into a prayer exercise; you can simply listen, stop, or cry wherever you need to.

steps.why: Start here because the listener’s question closely echoes yours: grief makes belief feel doubtful and prayer feel like “just talking or thinking to myself.” Tom Wright responds without minimizing the loss, saying, “God loves your broken heart,” and points to Mary and Martha’s words, “If you’d been here, my dad wouldn’t have died,” before offering the Psalms as a way to pray when you cannot manufacture your own words.

This clip stays with the physical reality of mourning rather than correcting it. The speaker centers John 11:35—“Jesus wept”—and says that if grief were wrong, Jesus would have sinned. He connects grief with love and distinguishes grieving “with hope” from being told not to grieve at all, which may help loosen the pressure to be composed three weeks after your mother’s death.
steps.episodeTitle: Some Things I Wish Everyone Knew About Grief

steps.why: Now the tour gives you permission to speak honestly instead of pretending. The hosts say the Bible’s response to suffering is “lament,” not to “ignore” it, “sweep it under the rug,” or explain it away. A guest describing his own grief then names the difference between the “actual presence of God” and the “perceived presence of God”—a careful acknowledgment that God’s nearness may not be something you can feel right now.

This is a stark companion for the days when prayer feels angry, accusing, or impossible. In Psalm 88, the speaker quotes, “My eyes are dim with grief,” and notes that the psalmist both attributes suffering to God and still says, “I call to you, Lord, every day.” The clip does not resolve that contradiction; it describes lament as demanding that God act consistently with the goodness he has claimed.
steps.episodeTitle: Lamentations Overview: What is a Lament?

steps.why: End with a quieter, longer horizon rather than a demand for immediate recovery. This conversation treats Jesus’ “blessed are those who grieve” as grief over actual death and loss, and describes comfort as the future arrival of restoration—a time when “you don’t need to grieve anymore.” It lets your present sorrow remain real while placing hope beyond it, not using hope to deny what has happened.
steps.episodeTitle: Sermon on the Mount E5: The Powerless, Grieving, and Unimportant

tour.closing: There is no required conclusion to reach here. If all you can do is hear someone say that your broken heart is not selfish, that Jesus wept, and that the Bible makes room for words you cannot yet form, this tour has done its work. For now, silence may be all you have; you do not have to turn it into a tidy prayer.

caveats: Clips on ad-inserted hosts (Megaphone: ask-nt-wright, spoken-gospel) can land up to ~2 minutes off against today’s stream. This is a known corpus-wide drift, not a bug in this tour.
A tour is model output over machine transcripts. The "why" text should report what a transcript says; it is not a claim that the speaker is right.

The player streams each episode straight from its publisher. A few hosts (Substack’s CDN, for one) refuse hotlinked requests and the step will say so and offer the URL instead — the clip boundaries are still good, the playback path is not.
